# Day 3 — Consolidation {#sec-day3-consolidation}

**20 minutes · plenary**

## Say it in one sentence

Without notes, write the sentence you would say to a colleague who asks what
`lm()` does. It must name the loss being minimised, say how the minimum is
found, and contain one number from today.

A sentence that meets the bar:

> It finds the intercept and slope with the smallest mean squared error — for
> our 80 patients, 110.3 and 0.289 — by solving two equations exactly rather
> than by searching, and the result would be a different line if we had chosen
> to minimise absolute error instead.

Count how many of the three elements your own sentence has.

## Four routes, one answer

Today's slope was computed four ways. Fill in what each cost and what each
required.

| Method | Where | Exact? | Needs |
|---|---|---|---|
| `lm()` / `LinearRegression` | @sec-supervised-learning | yes | nothing from you |
| grid search over 15,251 candidates | @sec-loss-functions | no, 0.30 against 0.2887 | a range that already contains the answer |
| gradient descent | @sec-gradient-descent | to five figures, after 50 steps | a learning rate, a starting point, standardised columns |
| closed form $\operatorname{Cov}(x,y)/\operatorname{Var}(x)$ | @sec-ols | yes, to machine precision | $\operatorname{Var}(x) > 0$ |

: {tbl-colwidths="[34,20,22,24]"}

The one that scales to the models you will meet after this module is the third,
which is also the only one that can fail silently.

## Self-assessment

Tick honestly. Anything unticked is what to review before Day 4.

- [ ] I can say what the learning algorithm contributes and what the dataset contributes.
- [ ] I can compute SSR, MSE, RMSE and MAE from residuals, in either language.
- [ ] I can explain why squaring makes a fit sensitive to three contaminated rows.
- [ ] I can write the gradient descent update rule, including the minus sign, from memory.
- [ ] I can tell from a loss curve whether a learning rate is too large or too small.
- [ ] I can derive $\hat\beta_0 = \bar{y} - \hat\beta_1\bar{x}$ without looking it up.
- [ ] I can state why the fitted residuals of a least-squares model sum to zero.

## Five questions

Answer in a sentence each.

1. A colleague fits glucose on age, reports a slope of 0.29, and concludes that
   age does not matter clinically. Give two separate reasons that conclusion is
   not supported — one about the number, one about what was never computed.
2. Tripling three glucose readings out of 80 flipped the fitted slope from
   positive to negative, while the least-absolute-error line did not move at
   all. Which of the two lines is correct?
3. Your gradient descent reports a loss that fell at every iteration and
   parameters that are nowhere near `lm()`'s. What has happened, and what is the
   first thing you change?
4. The OLS derivation divides by $\operatorname{Var}(x)$. What happens to the
   estimate as that variance shrinks, and what does that imply about comparing
   a coefficient from a narrow age band with one from a wide one?
5. If `lm()` solves the problem exactly in microseconds, why does any software
   use gradient descent at all?

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Answers.** (1) The number has no units attached in the claim and no comparison
— 0.29 mg/dL per year over 60 years of age is about 17 mg/dL, which is not
nothing; and nobody computed a held-out error or a baseline comparison, so the
claim rests on an in-sample fit. Accept either half as half marks. (2) Neither
and both: each is the best line under its own loss, and the question "which is
correct" is not well posed until someone says what errors cost. Students who
answer "the robust one" have half the point; press them on what they would do if
the three tripled values were real measurements. (3) It has converged along one
parameter and crawled along the other, because the columns are on very different
scales; standardise first, then revisit the learning rate. (4) The estimate
becomes unstable and can be many times larger — our 21-to-30 band gave 4.17
against 0.29 for the full range; coefficients are only comparable across studies
whose predictor ranges are comparable. (5) Because the closed form exists only
for squared error with a linear model, and because inverting $X^\top X$ is
infeasible once $X$ has a very large number of columns.

**Rubric** (if the day is assessed, 20 marks):

| | Marks |
|---|---|
| Fitted model and both baseline comparisons reported, in-sample status stated | 4 |
| All four losses computed correctly from residuals | 3 |
| Contaminated refit, with the two losses' lines compared and the mechanism explained | 4 |
| Gradient descent implemented, converging, and checked against `lm()` | 4 |
| Closed form derived by hand and verified numerically | 3 |
| One sentence naming the loss, the method and a number | 2 |

: {tbl-colwidths="[80,20]"}

Mark the explanation, not the arithmetic. A student whose descent did not
converge but who diagnosed why has understood more than one who copied a working
loop.
:::
:::

## What carries into Day 4

Three loose ends were left deliberately, and each opens the next session.

1. **Every number today was in-sample.** No split, no held-out patient, no
   evidence of generalisation. Day 5 brings the metrics back, and the tree that
   looked best on these 80 rows is the first casualty.
2. **The outcome was continuous.** Squared error is defined because the
   difference between a prediction and an outcome is a number. When the outcome
   is a diagnosis — positive or negative — subtraction stops meaning anything,
   and a new loss is needed. That is @sec-logistic-regression.
3. **The loss was chosen for us.** We showed that the choice changes the answer
   and then went back to squared error anyway, because it is differentiable.
   Day 4's loss is chosen for the same reason, and it is worth noticing that
   convenience keeps winning.
